For each integer \(s\ge 3\), let \(D_s\) be the least positive integer \(d\) with the following property: for every collection of \(2^s-2\) Borel probability measures on \(\mathbb R^d\), each absolutely continuous with respect to \(d\)-dimensional Lebesgue measure, there exist two affine hyperplanes whose complement has exactly four connected components, each having measure \(1/4\) for every measure in the collection. The same pair of hyperplanes must work for all the measures, and no perpendicularity condition is imposed. What is the exact value of \(D_s\) as a function of \(s\)?

7	In particular, the dimension-counting lower bound \(3(2^s-2)/2\) is **not** sufficient. The lower bound below uses explicit Gaussian measures; the upper bound uses a parity argument and a dimension-reduction argument.
8	
9	## 1. A parity lemma
10	
11	We need the following form of the two-variable Borsuk–Ulam argument.
12	
13	**Lemma 1.** Suppose \(a,b,r\) are positive integers satisfying
14	\[
15	a,b\ge r,\qquad a+b=3r.
16	\]
17	Let
18	\[
19	F=(F_1,F_2,F_3):S^a\times S^b\longrightarrow
20	\mathbb R^r\oplus\mathbb R^r\oplus\mathbb R^r
21	\]
22	be continuous, with
23	\[
24	\begin{aligned}
25	F(-u,v)&=(-F_1(u,v),F_2(u,v),-F_3(u,v)),\\
26	F(u,-v)&=(F_1(u,v),-F_2(u,v),-F_3(u,v)).
27	\end{aligned}
28	\]
29	If \(\binom r{a-r}\) is odd, then \(F\) has a zero.
30	
31	**Proof.** Here is the mod-two zero-count argument, including the required count.
32	
33	The group generated by the two antipodal maps acts freely on \(S^a\times S^b\). For a generic smooth map with the displayed symmetries, zeros are isolated, and we count their group orbits modulo two. This parity is invariant under equivariant homotopy: after a generic perturbation of the homotopy, its zero set modulo the group is a compact one-dimensional manifold whose boundary consists of the zero orbits at the two endpoints. A compact one-dimensional manifold has an even number of boundary points. Equivariant perturbations are possible because the action is free: perturb locally and copy the perturbation to its translates.
34	
35	Compute this parity using a particular map. Take the first \(r\) components to be independent linear forms in \(u\), the next \(r\) independent linear forms in \(v\), and the last \(r\) to be
36	\[
37	\ell_i(u)m_i(v),\qquad 1\le i\le r,
38	\]
39	with all forms in general position.
40	
41	The first two blocks restrict the projective variables to
42	\[
43	\mathbb {RP}^{a-r}\times\mathbb {RP}^{b-r}.
44	\]
45	For each last-block equation, either \(\ell_i(u)=0\) or \(m_i(v)=0\). General position and
46	\((a-r)+(b-r)=r\) imply that a zero is obtained precisely by choosing \(a-r\) equations of the first kind and the remaining \(b-r\) of the second kind. Each choice gives exactly one projective zero, and all are regular. Thus the parity is
47	\[
48	\binom r{a-r}\pmod2.
49	\]
50	If this is odd, a zero-free map is impossible. Continuous maps follow by approximation. ∎
51	
52	## 2. The upper bound
53	
54	Put
55	\[
56	m=2^{s-1}.
57	\]
58	We first show that \(2m-1\) measures in \(\mathbb R^{3m-1}\) can be equipartitioned by two hyperplanes.
59	
60	An oriented affine hyperplane in \(\mathbb R^D\) is parametrized by
61	\[
62	u=(u_0,\ldots,u_D)\in S^D,
63	\qquad
64	u_0+\sum_{\ell=1}^D u_\ell x_\ell=0.
65	\]
66	The two points with zero spatial normal are interpreted as constant positive or negative half-spaces.
67	
68	For an absolutely continuous probability measure \(\mu_i\), define
69	\[
70	\begin{aligned}
71	f_i(u,v)&=\int \operatorname{sgn}(u_0+u'\cdot x)\,d\mu_i(x),\\
72	g_i(u,v)&=\int \operatorname{sgn}(v_0+v'\cdot x)\,d\mu_i(x),\\
73	h_i(u,v)&=\int \operatorname{sgn}(u_0+u'\cdot x)
74	                 \operatorname{sgn}(v_0+v'\cdot x)\,d\mu_i(x).
75	\end{aligned}
76	\]
77	These functions are continuous, including at the constant half-spaces, by dominated convergence. They have the symmetries of Lemma 1.
78	
79	A simultaneous zero means that each of the four sign combinations has probability \(1/4\), since its probability is
80	\[
81	\frac14(1\pm f_i\pm g_i\pm h_i),
82	\]
83	with the corresponding signs.
84	
85	Apply the lemma with
86	\[
87	r=2m-1,\qquad a=3m-2,\qquad b=3m-1,
88	\]
89	restricting the first hyperplane parameter to any great \(S^a\subset S^b\). The necessary coefficient is
90	\[
91	\binom{2m-1}{m-1}.
92	\]
93	It is odd: \(2m=2^s\), and over \(\mathbb F_2\),
94	\[
95	(1+t)^{2m-1}=1+t+\cdots+t^{2m-1}.
96	\]
97	Consequently,
98	\[
99	\Delta(2m-1,2)\le 3m-1,                                      \tag{1}
100	\]
101	where \(\Delta(q,2)\) denotes the dimension needed for \(q\) measures and two hyperplanes.
102	
103	We now prove the dimension-reduction inequality used here.
104	
105	**Lemma 2.**
106	\[
107	\Delta(q,2)\le \Delta(q+1,2)-1.
108	\]
109	
110	**Proof.** Suppose \(q+1\) measures can always be equipartitioned in \(\mathbb R^{d+1}\). Embed the given \(q\) measures in
111	\[
112	L=\mathbb R^d\times\{0\}.
113	\]
114	For \(\varepsilon>0\), thicken each into a product with the uniform measure on \([-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]\). Add uniform probability measure on \(B(p,\varepsilon)\), where \(p\notin L\).
115	
116	Choose an equipartition. Each hyperplane bisects the added measure, so intersects \(B(p,\varepsilon)\). Normalize its spatial normal to have length one. Its offset is then bounded, and as \(\varepsilon\to0\) we may take a convergent subsequence of both hyperplanes. Both limiting hyperplanes pass through \(p\).
117	
118	Neither limit can contain \(L\): the only ambient hyperplane containing \(L\) is \(L\) itself, and \(p\notin L\). Thus their restrictions to \(L\) are genuine affine hyperplanes. Dominated convergence, using the absolute continuity of the original measures, shows that their four sign regions each have measure \(1/4\).
119	
120	These regions cannot include an empty one. Hence the restricted hyperplanes have exactly four complementary components. ∎
121	
122	Combining (1) with Lemma 2 gives
123	\[
124	D_s\le 3m-2.                                                \tag{2}
125	\]
126	
127	## 3. The algebraic construction for the lower bound
128	
129	The crucial fact is the following explicit construction.
130	
131	**Lemma 3.** For every even \(m\ge4\), there are \(2m-2\) positive definite real symmetric \(m\times m\) matrices
132	\[
133	A_1,\ldots,A_{2m-2}
134	\]
135	such that
136	\[
137	u^TA_i v=0\quad\text{for all }i
138	\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u=0\text{ or }v=0.                \tag{3}
139	\]
140	
141	**Proof.** Write \(m=2k\), where \(k\ge2\), and identify \(\mathbb R^m\) with the space of complex polynomials of degree at most \(k-1\).
142	
143	Set
144	\[
145	h(t)=\prod_{\ell=1}^{2k-2}(t+\ell).
146	\]
147	For each subset \(S\subset\{1,\ldots,2k-2\}\) of size \(k-1\), let \(a_S,b_S\in\mathbb R^k\) be the coefficient vectors of
148	\[
149	\prod_{\ell\in S}(t+\ell),\qquad
150	\prod_{\ell\notin S}(t+\ell).
151	\]
152	Their coefficients are strictly positive, so
153	\[
154	a_S\cdot b_S>0.                                             \tag{4}
155	\]
156	The two monic polynomials have disjoint, nonempty root sets, so their coefficient vectors are not proportional.
157	
158	Choose a real skew-symmetric matrix \(K\) such that
159	\[
160	a_S^TKb_S\ne0\quad\text{for every }S.                       \tag{5}
161	\]
162	For completeness, here is an entirely explicit integer choice. Put
163	\[
164	H=(2k-1)!,\qquad T=2H^2+2,
165	\]
166	enumerate the pairs \(0\le i<j<k\) by \(e=0,1,\ldots\), and set
167	\[
168	K_{ij}=T^e,\qquad K_{ji}=-T^e.
169	\]
170	Every coefficient of \(a_S,b_S\) is at most \(H\). Therefore
171	\[
172	a_S^TKb_S
173	=\sum_{i<j}(a_i b_j-a_j b_i)T^{e(i,j)}
174	\]
175	is a nonzero integer polynomial evaluated at \(T\), with coefficients of absolute value at most \(H^2\). Its leading nonzero term exceeds the sum of the absolute values of all lower terms because \(T-1>H^2\). This proves (5).
176	
177	For complex coefficient vectors \(z,w\), define a real symmetric bilinear map \(B\) whose components are:
178	
179	1. \(\operatorname{Re}(z^*w)\);
180	2. \(\operatorname{Re}(z^*iKw)\);
181	3. the real and imaginary parts of every coefficient of
182	   \[
183	   z(t)w(t)\pmod {h(t)}.
184	   \]
185	
186	The remainder has \(2k-2\) complex coefficients. Thus \(B\) has
187	\[
188	2+2(2k-2)=4k-2=2m-2
189	\]
190	real components. Symmetry of its second component follows because \(iK\) is Hermitian.
191	
192	We claim
193	\[
194	B(z,w)=0\Longrightarrow z=0\text{ or }w=0.                 \tag{6}
195	\]
196	Otherwise the remainder condition gives
197	\[
198	z(t)w(t)=\lambda h(t),\qquad \lambda\ne0.
199	\]
200	Both factors have degree \(k-1\). Since \(h\) has distinct real roots, for some complementary root partition,
201	\[
202	z=\alpha a_S,\qquad w=\beta b_S,\qquad \alpha\beta\ne0.
203	\]
204	The first two components of \(B\) are then
205	\[
206	(a_S\cdot b_S)\operatorname{Re}(\bar\alpha\beta),
207	\qquad
208	-(a_S^TKb_S)\operatorname{Im}(\bar\alpha\beta).
209	\]
210	By (4) and (5), their vanishing forces \(\bar\alpha\beta=0\), a contradiction.
211	
212	Represent the components of \(B\) by symmetric matrices
213	\[
214	C_1=I,\ C_2,\ldots,C_{2m-2}.
215	\]
216	Choose
217	\[
218	R_i> \max_a\sum_b |(C_i)_{ab}|,
219	\qquad
220	A_1=I,\quad A_i=R_iI+C_i\quad(i\ge2).
221	\]
222	Each \(A_i\) is positive definite by strict diagonal dominance. If all \(u^TA_iv\) vanish, the equation for \(A_1\) gives \(u^Tv=0\), and the remaining equations give \(u^TC_iv=0\). Now (6) proves (3). ∎
223	
224	## 4. Gaussian measures give the matching lower bound
225	
226	Continue with \(m=2^{s-1}\), and put
227	\[
228	j=2m-2,\qquad d_0=3m-3.
229	\]
230	Decompose
231	\[
232	\mathbb R^{d_0}=L\oplus W,\qquad
233	\dim L=j-1=2m-3,\quad \dim W=m.
234	\]
235	
236	Take \(j\) Gaussian measures with means
237	\[
238	c_1=0,\qquad c_i=e_{i-1}\in L\quad(2\le i\le j)
239	\]
240	and covariance matrices
241	\[
242	\Sigma_i=I_L\oplus A_i,
243	\]
244	where the \(A_i\) are supplied by Lemma 3. These are nondegenerate Gaussians, hence absolutely continuous.
245	
246	Suppose two hyperplanes equipartitioned them.
247	
248	An affine hyperplane bisects a nondegenerate Gaussian exactly when it passes through its mean: its normal projection is a one-dimensional Gaussian, whose unique median is its mean. Both hyperplanes must therefore contain all \(c_i\). Their offsets are zero and their nonzero normals \(u,v\) lie in \(W\).
249	
250	For a centered bivariate Gaussian with correlation \(\rho\),
251	\[
252	\Pr(X>0,Y>0)=\frac14+\frac{1}{2\pi}\arcsin\rho.              \tag{7}
253	\]
254	This follows by writing the pair as two linear projections of a rotationally symmetric planar Gaussian and measuring the corresponding angular wedge. The degenerate cases \(\rho=\pm1\) also plainly cannot give four equal quadrants.
255	
256	Thus four equal quadrants for the \(i\)-th Gaussian require zero covariance:
257	\[
258	u^T\Sigma_i v=u^TA_i v=0.
259	\]
260	This holds for every \(i\), contradicting Lemma 3.
261	
262	Consequently, the required property fails in dimension \(3m-3\). The property is monotone in dimension: project measures onto a lower-dimensional coordinate space and lift an equipartition back. Hence failure in dimension \(3m-3\) implies
263	\[
264	D_s\ge3m-2.                                                \tag{8}
265	\]
266	Together, (2) and (8) prove the stated answer.
267	
268	## 5. Exact Python verification
269	
270	The following uses integer arithmetic only. It constructs the bilinear forms and positive definite covariance blocks, verifies their identities on **every pair of basis vectors**, checks the finite factorization certificates, and checks the upper-bound parity coefficient.
271	
272	The general proof above handles all \(s\); this parameterized code checks each finite instance. I ran it for \(s=3,4,5\).
273	
274	```python
275	from itertools import combinations
276	from math import factorial, comb
277	
278	# Polynomials are coefficient lists, constant coefficient first.
279	def trim(p):
280	    p = list(p)
281	    while len(p) > 1 and p[-1] == 0:
282	        p.pop()
283	    return p
284	
285	def add(p, q, sign=1):
286	    r = [0] * max(len(p), len(q))
287	    for i, x in enumerate(p):
288	        r[i] += x
289	    for i, x in enumerate(q):
290	        r[i] += sign * x
291	    return trim(r)
292	
293	def mul(p, q):
294	    r = [0] * (len(p) + len(q) - 1)
295	    for i, x in enumerate(p):
296	        for j, y in enumerate(q):
297	            r[i+j] += x*y
298	    return trim(r)
299	
300	def divrem(p, h):
301	    assert h[-1] == 1
302	    r = trim(p)
303	    q = [0] * max(1, len(r) - len(h) + 1)
304	    while len(r) >= len(h) and r != [0]:
305	        t, c = len(r) - len(h), r[-1]
306	        q[t] = c
307	        for i, x in enumerate(h):
308	            r[t+i] -= c*x
309	        r = trim(r)
310	    assert add(mul(q, h), r) == trim(p)
311	    return trim(q), r
312	
313	def rootpoly(S):
314	    p = [1]
315	    for x in S:
316	        p = mul(p, [x, 1])
317	    return p
318	
319	def dot(x, y):
320	    return sum(a*b for a, b in zip(x, y))
321	
322	def bil(x, M, y):
323	    return sum(x[i]*M[i][j]*y[j]
324	               for i in range(len(x)) for j in range(len(y)))
325	
326	def zeros(n):
327	    return [[0]*n for _ in range(n)]
328	
329	def check(s):
330	    assert s >= 3
331	    m = 2**(s-1)
332	    k, j = m//2, 2*m-2
333	    H = factorial(2*k-1)
334	    T = 2*H*H + 2
335	
336	    K = zeros(k)
337	    e = 0
338	    for a in range(k):
339	        for b in range(a+1, k):
340	            K[a][b], K[b][a] = T**e, -T**e
341	            e += 1
342	
343	    h = rootpoly(range(1, 2*k-1))
344	    assert T-1 > H*H
345	
346	    # Exhaust all complementary factorizations of h.
347	    U = set(range(1, 2*k-1))
348	    certificates = 0
349	    for S in combinations(sorted(U), k-1):
350	        a = rootpoly(S)
351	        b = rootpoly(sorted(U-set(S)))
352	        assert mul(a, b) == h
353	        assert min(a+b) > 0 and max(a+b) <= H
354	        assert dot(a, b) > 0
355	
356	        wedge = [a[r]*b[t] - a[t]*b[r]
357	                 for r in range(k) for t in range(r+1, k)]
358	        assert any(wedge)
359	        assert max(map(abs, wedge)) <= H*H
360	        value = sum(c*T**e for e, c in enumerate(wedge))
361	        assert value == bil(a, K, b) != 0
362	        certificates += 1
363	
364	    I = zeros(m)
365	    for a in range(m):
366	        I[a][a] = 1
367	
368	    # Real coordinates are (Re z, Im z).
369	    C2 = zeros(m)
370	    for a in range(k):
371	        for b in range(k):
372	            C2[a][k+b] = -K[a][b]
373	            C2[k+a][b] = K[a][b]
374	    C = [I, C2]
375	
376	    rem = [divrem([0]*e + [1], h)[1]
377	           for e in range(2*k-1)]
378	
379	    # Real and imaginary coefficient forms of z(t)w(t) mod h.
380	    for r in range(2*k-2):
381	        R, J = zeros(m), zeros(m)
382	        for a in range(k):
383	            for b in range(k):
384	                v = rem[a+b][r] if r < len(rem[a+b]) else 0
385	                R[a][b], R[k+a][k+b] = v, -v
386	                J[a][k+b], J[k+a][b] = v, v
387	        C.extend([R, J])
388	
389	    assert len(C) == j
390	    assert all(Q[a][b] == Q[b][a]
391	               for Q in C for a in range(m) for b in range(m))
392	
393	    # Independently check the bilinear formula on ALL basis pairs.
394	    # Because the formulas are bilinear, these checks are universal.
395	    for a in range(m):
396	        for b in range(m):
397	            x = [int(t == a) for t in range(m)]
398	            y = [int(t == b) for t in range(m)]
399	            xr, xi, yr, yi = x[:k], x[k:], y[:k], y[k:]
400	            pr = add(mul(xr, yr), mul(xi, yi), -1)
401	            pi = add(mul(xr, yi), mul(xi, yr))
402	            rr, ri = divrem(pr, h)[1], divrem(pi, h)[1]
403	            expected = [dot(x, y),
404	                        bil(xi, K, yr) - bil(xr, K, yi)]
405	            for r in range(2*k-2):
406	                expected.extend([
407	                    rr[r] if r < len(rr) else 0,
408	                    ri[r] if r < len(ri) else 0
409	                ])
410	            assert expected == [Q[a][b] for Q in C]
411	
412	    # Positive definite covariance blocks, with exact certificates.
413	    A = [I]
414	    for Q in C[1:]:
415	        R = 1 + max(sum(abs(v) for v in row) for row in Q)
416	        P = [[Q[a][b] + (R if a == b else 0)
417	              for b in range(m)] for a in range(m)]
418	        assert all(
419	            P[a][a] > sum(abs(P[a][b])
420	                          for b in range(m) if b != a)
421	            for a in range(m)
422	        )
423	        assert all(P[a][b] - R*I[a][b] == Q[a][b]
424	                   for a in range(m) for b in range(m))
425	        A.append(P)
426	    assert len(A) == j
427	
428	    # Upper-bound parity and both dimension calculations.
429	    r, a, b = 2*m-1, 3*m-2, 3*m-1
430	    assert a+b == 3*r
431	    assert comb(r, a-r) % 2 == 1
432	    d0 = (j-1) + m
433	    assert d0 == 3*m-3
434	    assert b-1 == d0+1
435	
436	    print(f"s={s}: j={j}; factor certificates={certificates}; "
437	          f"forms={len(C)}; counterexample dimension={d0}; "
438	          f"upper dimension={b-1}")
439	    return C, A
440	
441	for s in (3, 4, 5):

443	```

7	## 1. A parity lemma
8	
9	We need the following form of the two-variable Borsuk–Ulam argument.
10	
11	**Lemma 1.** Suppose \(a,b,r\) are positive integers satisfying
12	\[
13	a,b\ge r,\qquad a+b=3r.
14	\]
15	Let
16	\[
17	F=(F_1,F_2,F_3):S^a\times S^b\longrightarrow
18	\mathbb R^r\oplus\mathbb R^r\oplus\mathbb R^r
19	\]
20	be continuous, with
21	\[
22	\begin{aligned}
23	F(-u,v)&=(-F_1(u,v),F_2(u,v),-F_3(u,v)),\\
24	F(u,-v)&=(F_1(u,v),-F_2(u,v),-F_3(u,v)).
25	\end{aligned}
26	\]
27	If \(\binom r{a-r}\) is odd, then \(F\) has a zero.
28	
29	**Proof.** Here is the mod-two zero-count argument, including the required count.
30	
31	The group generated by the two antipodal maps acts freely on \(S^a\times S^b\). For a generic smooth map with the displayed symmetries, zeros are isolated, and we count their group orbits modulo two. This parity is invariant under equivariant homotopy: after a generic perturbation of the homotopy, its zero set modulo the group is a compact one-dimensional manifold whose boundary consists of the zero orbits at the two endpoints. A compact one-dimensional manifold has an even number of boundary points. Equivariant perturbations are possible because the action is free: perturb locally and copy the perturbation to its translates.
32	
33	Compute this parity using a particular map. Take the first \(r\) components to be independent linear forms in \(u\), the next \(r\) independent linear forms in \(v\), and the last \(r\) to be
34	\[
35	\ell_i(u)m_i(v),\qquad 1\le i\le r,
36	\]
37	with all forms in general position.
38	
39	The first two blocks restrict the projective variables to
40	\[
41	\mathbb {RP}^{a-r}\times\mathbb {RP}^{b-r}.
42	\]
43	For each last-block equation, either \(\ell_i(u)=0\) or \(m_i(v)=0\). General position and
44	\((a-r)+(b-r)=r\) imply that a zero is obtained precisely by choosing \(a-r\) equations of the first kind and the remaining \(b-r\) of the second kind. Each choice gives exactly one projective zero, and all are regular. Thus the parity is
45	\[
46	\binom r{a-r}\pmod2.
47	\]
48	If this is odd, a zero-free map is impossible. Continuous maps follow by approximation. ∎

50	## 2. The upper bound
51	
52	Put
53	\[
54	m=2^{s-1}.
55	\]
56	We first show that \(2m-1\) measures in \(\mathbb R^{3m-1}\) can be equipartitioned by two hyperplanes.
57	
58	An oriented affine hyperplane in \(\mathbb R^D\) is parametrized by
59	\[
60	u=(u_0,\ldots,u_D)\in S^D,
61	\qquad
62	u_0+\sum_{\ell=1}^D u_\ell x_\ell=0.
63	\]
64	The two points with zero spatial normal are interpreted as constant positive or negative half-spaces.
65	
66	For an absolutely continuous probability measure \(\mu_i\), define
67	\[
68	\begin{aligned}
69	f_i(u,v)&=\int \operatorname{sgn}(u_0+u'\cdot x)\,d\mu_i(x),\\
70	g_i(u,v)&=\int \operatorname{sgn}(v_0+v'\cdot x)\,d\mu_i(x),\\
71	h_i(u,v)&=\int \operatorname{sgn}(u_0+u'\cdot x)
72	                 \operatorname{sgn}(v_0+v'\cdot x)\,d\mu_i(x).
73	\end{aligned}
74	\]
75	These functions are continuous, including at the constant half-spaces, by dominated convergence. They have the symmetries of Lemma 1.
76	
77	A simultaneous zero means that each of the four sign combinations has probability \(1/4\), since its probability is
78	\[
79	\frac14(1\pm f_i\pm g_i\pm h_i),
80	\]
81	with the corresponding signs.
82	
83	Apply the lemma with
84	\[
85	r=2m-1,\qquad a=3m-2,\qquad b=3m-1,
86	\]

88	\[
89	\binom{2m-1}{m-1}.
90	\]
91	It is odd: \(2m=2^s\), and over \(\mathbb F_2\),
92	\[
93	(1+t)^{2m-1}=1+t+\cdots+t^{2m-1}.
94	\]
95	Consequently,
96	\[
97	\Delta(2m-1,2)\le 3m-1,                                      \tag{1}
98	\]
99	where \(\Delta(q,2)\) denotes the dimension needed for \(q\) measures and two hyperplanes.

101	We now prove the dimension-reduction inequality used here.
102	
103	**Lemma 2.**
104	\[
105	\Delta(q,2)\le \Delta(q+1,2)-1.
106	\]
107	
108	**Proof.** Suppose \(q+1\) measures can always be equipartitioned in \(\mathbb R^{d+1}\). Embed the given \(q\) measures in
109	\[
110	L=\mathbb R^d\times\{0\}.
111	\]
112	For \(\varepsilon>0\), thicken each into a product with the uniform measure on \([-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]\). Add uniform probability measure on \(B(p,\varepsilon)\), where \(p\notin L\).
113	
114	Choose an equipartition. Each hyperplane bisects the added measure, so intersects \(B(p,\varepsilon)\). Normalize its spatial normal to have length one. Its offset is then bounded, and as \(\varepsilon\to0\) we may take a convergent subsequence of both hyperplanes. Both limiting hyperplanes pass through \(p\).

116	Neither limit can contain \(L\): the only ambient hyperplane containing \(L\) is \(L\) itself, and \(p\notin L\). Thus their restrictions to \(L\) are genuine affine hyperplanes. 117	
118	These regions cannot include an empty one. Hence the restricted hyperplanes have exactly four complementary components. ∎

125	## 3. The algebraic construction for the lower bound
126	
127	The crucial fact is the following explicit construction.
128	
129	**Lemma 3.** For every even \(m\ge4\), there are \(2m-2\) positive definite real symmetric \(m\times m\) matrices
130	\[
131	A_1,\ldots,A_{2m-2}
132	\]
133	such that
134	\[
135	u^TA_i v=0\quad\text{for all }i
136	\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u=0\text{ or }v=0.                \tag{3}
137	\]
138	
139	**Proof.** Write \(m=2k\), where \(k\ge2\), and identify \(\mathbb R^m\) with the space of complex polynomials of degree at most \(k-1\).
140	
141	Set
142	\[
143	h(t)=\prod_{\ell=1}^{2k-2}(t+\ell).
144	\]
145	For each subset \(S\subset\{1,\ldots,2k-2\}\) of size \(k-1\), let \(a_S,b_S\in\mathbb R^k\) be the coefficient vectors of
146	\[
147	\prod_{\ell\in S}(t+\ell),\qquad
148	\prod_{\ell\notin S}(t+\ell).
149	\]
150	Their coefficients are strictly positive, so
151	\[
152	a_S\cdot b_S>0.                                             \tag{4}
153	\]
154	The two monic polynomials have disjoint, nonempty root sets, so their coefficient vectors are not proportional.
155	
156	Choose a real skew-symmetric matrix \(K\) such that
157	\[
158	a_S^TKb_S\ne0\quad\text{for every }S.                       \tag{5}
159	\]
160	For completeness, here is an entirely explicit integer choice. Put
161	\[
162	H=(2k-1)!,\qquad T=2H^2+2,
163	\]
164	enumerate the pairs \(0\le i<j<k\) by \(e=0,1,\ldots\), and set
165	\[
166	K_{ij}=T^e,\qquad K_{ji}=-T^e.
167	\]
168	Every coefficient of \(a_S,b_S\) is at most \(H\). Therefore
169	\[
170	a_S^TKb_S
171	=\sum_{i<j}(a_i b_j-a_j b_i)T^{e(i,j)}
172	\]
173	is a nonzero integer polynomial evaluated at \(T\), with coefficients of absolute value at most \(H^2\). Its leading nonzero term exceeds the sum of the absolute values of all lower terms because \(T-1>H^2\). This proves (5).
174	
175	For complex coefficient vectors \(z,w\), define a real symmetric bilinear map \(B\) whose components are:
176	
177	1. \(\operatorname{Re}(z^*w)\);
178	2. \(\operatorname{Re}(z^*iKw)\);
179	3. the real and imaginary parts of every coefficient of
180	   \[
181	   z(t)w(t)\pmod {h(t)}.
182	   \]
183	
184	The remainder has \(2k-2\) complex coefficients. Thus \(B\) has
185	\[
186	2+2(2k-2)=4k-2=2m-2
187	\]
188	real components. Symmetry of its second component follows because \(iK\) is Hermitian.
189	
190	We claim
191	\[
192	B(z,w)=0\Longrightarrow z=0\text{ or }w=0.                 \tag{6}
193	\]
194	Otherwise the remainder condition gives
195	\[
196	z(t)w(t)=\lambda h(t),\qquad \lambda\ne0.
197	\]
198	Both factors have degree \(k-1\). Since \(h\) has distinct real roots, for some complementary root partition,
199	\[
200	z=\alpha a_S,\qquad w=\beta b_S,\qquad \alpha\beta\ne0.
201	\]
202	The first two components of \(B\) are then
203	\[
204	(a_S\cdot b_S)\operatorname{Re}(\bar\alpha\beta),
205	\qquad
206	-(a_S^TKb_S)\operatorname{Im}(\bar\alpha\beta).
207	\]
208	By (4) and (5), their vanishing forces \(\bar\alpha\beta=0\), a contradiction.
209	
210	Represent the components of \(B\) by symmetric matrices
211	\[
212	C_1=I,\ C_2,\ldots,C_{2m-2}.
213	\]
214	Choose
215	\[
216	R_i> \max_a\sum_b |(C_i)_{ab}|,
217	\qquad
218	A_1=I,\quad A_i=R_iI+C_i\quad(i\ge2).
219	\]
220	Each \(A_i\) is positive definite by strict diagonal dominance. If all \(u^TA_iv\) vanish, the equation for \(A_1\) gives \(u^Tv=0\), and the remaining equations give \(u^TC_iv=0\). Now (6) proves (3). ∎

222	## 4. Gaussian measures give the matching lower bound
223	
224	Continue with \(m=2^{s-1}\), and put
225	\[
226	j=2m-2,\qquad d_0=3m-3.
227	\]
228	Decompose
229	\[
230	\mathbb R^{d_0}=L\oplus W,\qquad
231	\dim L=j-1=2m-3,\quad \dim W=m.
232	\]
233	
234	Take \(j\) Gaussian measures with means
235	\[
236	c_1=0,\qquad c_i=e_{i-1}\in L\quad(2\le i\le j)

239	\[

243	
244	Suppose two hyperplanes equipartitioned them.
245	
246	An affine hyperplane bisects a nondegenerate Gaussian exactly when it passes through its mean: its normal projection is a one-dimensional Gaussian, whose unique median is its mean. 248	For a centered bivariate Gaussian with correlation \(\rho\),
249	\[
250	\Pr(X>0,Y>0)=\frac14+\frac{1}{2\pi}\arcsin\rho.              \tag{7}

255	\[
256	u^T\Sigma_i v=u^TA_i v=0.

261	\[
262	D_s\ge3m-2.                                                \tag{8}
